Betyna Dorminier, figure clé à la MDJ-PA: Betyna Dorminier, a key figure at the MDJ-PAT, builds trust with youth by offering a listening ear, support and tools for their future.
Des jeunes ont rejoint Betyna lors de l': Youth joined Betyna at the On prend la rue event last year in Rivière-des-Prairies. Photo credit: Dave Nicolas.
À 15 ans, j’ai commencé à fréquenter la: At 15, I started going to the Maison des jeunes de Pointe-aux-Trembles. Betyna, Mike and other youth workers played an important part in my growth and in my inclusion in the area. When I left to live in Saguenay at 20, I couldn’t imagine not saying goodbye to them. Even today, I often visit them when I’m in Montréal.
J’ai choisi de faire un portrait de Bety: I chose to write a profile of Betyna because even though my relationship with her will always be “a young person and their youth worker,” and I’ll never know all sides of her, she’s an important person to me. Most of the youth of my generation, her first cohort, are still in touch with her. What we appreciate is that she doesn’t hesitate to reach out to invite us to events, like the year-end gala, or even to hang out together!
<strong>Betyna Dorminier est la co-coord: Betyna Dorminier is co-coordinator of the Maison des jeunes de Pointe-aux-Trembles (MDJ-PAT), in addition to being a youth worker. Since arriving in the neighbourhood in 2017, she has watched “her youth,” as she likes to call them, grow up and take flight into adulthood. They often come back to check in on her. We met Betyna at La Caverne, one of the MDJ-PAT’s two service points, to understand how the relationships she builds with young people create a bond of trust with them.
<strong>‍</strong>En ce mercredi de fin: ‍On this Wednesday in late July, there isn’t a cloud in sight, only a soft blue sky. We meet Betyna at the Maison des jeunes, located near Richelieu Park, a place full of nostalgia for the neighbourhood’s older residents: fights, flirting, basketball games, gatherings with friends… it all happened there. It’s 1 p.m., an hour before the little house turned drop-in space opens. The two co-coordinators, Cendrine and Betyna, are in the living room. One is on her computer, the other is eating lunch and waiting for us. On the wall near the entrance hangs a bulletin board decorated with photos: graduating youth, selfies from outings, friends laughing… They bear witness to the memories piled up over the years. We head to the second floor, to an office where it’s cooler.
Betyna grandit dans une famille haïtienn: Betyna grew up in a Haitian family as an only child. Her mother worked long hours to make sure her daughter never lacked food or clothes. “My mother is very generous. When people talk about her, they talk about her the same way they talk about me. They say ‘she’ll do anything for you.’ I guess I got that from her,” she says, sitting in a red armchair, legs crossed. In high school, she spent her school breaks and summers at her great-cousin’s place. “She was my second mother. I can say she’s the one who gave me love in the duo. My mother provided, and she gave me attention and love.”
Née à Montréal-Nord en 1996, Betyna est: Born in Montréal-Nord in 1996, Betyna is now a Pointelière at heart. In 2017, when she was 21, a childhood friend who was a youth worker at La Caverne offered her a job working alongside her. Right in the middle of questioning her university studies in mathematics and statistics at Concordia University, she accepted. “University just didn’t speak to me. Maybe I was biased because of the [program] I chose in the first place, I don’t know, but when I asked myself why I was there, I no longer had an answer.” She began her career as a part-time employee for the homework help program “Persévérance scolaire.”
Au fil des années, la jeune femme creuse: Over the years, the young woman carved out her place within the team. “I came [to the MDJ] because I was [looking for] a job, and in the end I found a passion.” Tutor, youth worker, co-coordinator… she has worn many hats in her eight years at the MDJ-PAT.
Avant ça, à 17 ans, elle a d'abord trava: Before that, at 17, she first worked at a day camp in Hochelaga called Clin d’œil. Surrounded by creative kids, she had allowed herself to invent a life. But when she arrived at the maison des jeunes eight years ago, she felt a jolt. The atmosphere was different from her old job. “[...] It was a clash, because these are youth who live the same reality as me,” she explains, placing her hand on her chest. “The jokes they tell, I laugh for real, it’s not a ‘hee-hee’ because I’m at day camp and I have to laugh with you. You say something, I can relate and I find it really funny, I can have real conversations with you about things that really happened to me!”
Les intervenants accompagnent les jeunes: Youth workers accompany young people to Montréal festivities, like the Grands Feux Loto-Québec. Photo credit: Dave Nicolas
Vêtue d’un chandail noir avec le logo de: Dressed in a black sweatshirt with the MDJ-PAT logo, she says she supervises a summer committee, run by the youth to organize summer activities. In the last 30 minutes of their group meetings, she always brings up topics like vulnerability, courage and leadership… “The first speech I gave was about respect. I asked ‘how does someone show you respect?’ and I got silence,” she says, visibly annoyed. “[…] I want to teach [them] concepts so they can carry them into their lives.” Through that question, the youth come to understand that respect can be subjective and depends on the relationships between people, Betyna explains.
Une question nous brûle les lèvres : pou: One question is burning on our lips: why does she want to teach life lessons to young people?
Derrière ses lunettes de vue transparent: Behind her clear prescription glasses, her gaze turns toward the window. “[Generally], my clientele is people like me, second-generation immigrants,” she says, bringing her eyes back to us. “They’re the people I have the best connections with, I understand everything about them.” From her observations, the teachings immigrant parents pass on are more conservative, far from the reality of Quebec schools. “Sometimes there’s a clash between home and school. Then the young person just feels misunderstood. A lot of them go to church and I know they’ve received certain teachings. I try to bring these three aspects together (teachings from home, school and church), to draw out what’s relevant, so that afterward, you make your own choices. I don’t want you to think you just have one destiny [...],” she says with a shrug.
Le lien de confiance que Betyna construi: The bond of trust Betyna builds lets some youth see her as a big sister and even a mother, she says. “If you have a panic at midnight, call me and I’ll come. It’s happened to me before.” That closeness also earns her the young people’s respect. “I want the young person to feel heard. My goal is that, in the long run, you tell me what’s going on and I’ll advise you. If I have a good relationship with you, I’ll even tell you what to do,” she says, her Tupperware in hand.
Si le jeune fait des choix avec lesquels: If a young person makes choices the youth worker doesn’t agree with, she still wants to know about them. That lets them assert themselves, she says, sitting at the edge of the armchair. She draws a parallel with the leaders at the church she attended when she was younger. “At church, I was known for my obedience, but if there was one thing that made me disobey, it was being asked to speak up front!” Like the time she didn’t show up to lead the youth service. “Did my leader scold me? Did he hit me? No! He came to see me and said ‘you didn’t come?’ What did he do? Nothing! Those are my choices! It fits with my basic approach, where I advise you, I tell you what to do, then you do what you want.”
Betyna raconte comment peut naître un li: Betyna describes how a bond of trust can begin with teenagers. “There’s a young girl I knew from a school who came to the MDJ. I said ‘hey, hi Sylvie!’ She looked at me and said ‘you know my name?’” Betyna recounts. “She asked me if that was a bad sign,” she confides, laughing. While this detail may seem trivial, it confirms to the youth that they’re not just people who come to the MDJ-PAT, but individuals in their own right. “I remember their names, I try to listen to them.”
Elle se rappelle cette fois où elle a ré: She recalls a time she managed to build a bond of trust with a young person who had been suspended from school. Her eyes drift toward the window. “He had a background, I think his school suspected him of selling drugs. He didn’t tell me his life story. Often, these aren’t youth who’ll put their business out there, their secrets. I didn’t say to him ‘what you’re doing is a crime.’ I’m here, I listen.” In that space, he confided that his brother was going to prison. “Sometimes I’d see him in the neighbourhood, he’d come here, say hi, but not really talk. When it started getting too crowded, he’d leave. Even if he doesn’t come and tell me his whole life, we made a connection!”
D’ailleurs, ce sont les jeunes les plus: Besides, it’s the shyest youth who surprise her, like David*. “Even if he doesn’t talk to me, I tell him I’m happy to see him. I think I’m making conversation, but I’m actually more conducting an interrogation,” she says with a half-smile. One day, he opened up to Betyna. He talked for a long time about a restaurant he had gone to, and after several minutes she wondered why he was talking so much. But the next morning, as she was getting ready for work, she realized it was the first time this young person had confided so much. “I’m investing in a relationship,” she told herself.
Ces liens, basés sur la confiance, peuve: These bonds, built on trust, can sometimes break. She leans back against the backrest of her armchair, her voice lowering. “It hurts me… but it’s a risk.” With a heavy heart, she describes a defining moment in her career. “Something happened in my young person’s life, there was an ‘explosion’ and I was part of it. I took a lot of heat. […] We were at homework help and he crashed out on me, in front of everyone,” Betyna continues. “I was shocked.”
Cependant, d’autres démontrent leur appr: Others, however, show their appreciation for Betyna. It’s common for her and her colleagues to be invited to graduation ceremonies, sports games and birthdays. “[These young people’s lives] aren’t the maison des jeunes. If you want to have an impact on someone’s life, you can’t stay in just one place.”
Betyna conclut l’entrevue et s’étonne du: Betyna wraps up the interview, surprised at how time has flown. We head back down to the main floor of La Caverne, where Cendrine is still sitting. Tomorrow is a big day: they’re going go-karting at Action 500 with the youth!
